Exam Blueprint (What Gets Tested)

The CDMP Reference & Master Data Management Specialist exam is 100 questions, 90 minutes, 60% pass mark (70%+ also earns a "Mastery" designation), and is open book (DMBOK2 + one additional reference permitted, as in all CDMP exams). Like all CDMP Specialist exams, it draws roughly 70% from the specialty area (Reference & Master Data, DMBOK2 Ch 10) and ~30% from supporting knowledge areas that connect to R&MD (Data Governance, Data Quality, Data Integration & Interoperability, Data Modeling/Architecture, Metadata).

⚠️ Accuracy note: The per-topic percentages below are estimated emphasis derived from the structure and length of DMBOK2 Chapter 10 — they are NOT official DAMA-published topic weights. DAMA publishes the specialty/supporting split (~70/30) and the question count, but does not publish a granular per-subtopic breakdown. Treat these as a study-prioritization guide, not exact exam quotas. Action item: confirm the current official format on the DAMA/CDMP exam page before your exam, as DAMA periodically updates exam specifications.

Estimated study emphasis (for prioritization only):

Topic Area Est. Emphasis Source DMBOK2 Chapter
R&MD Concepts, Data Classification, Drivers, Goals & Principles ~12% Specialty Ch 10
Reference Data Management (types, structures, standards, change control) ~14% Specialty Ch 10
Master Data Concepts, Subject Areas & MDM Activities ~14% Specialty Ch 10
Matching, Identity Resolution, Survivorship & Golden Records ~16% Specialty Ch 10
MDM Architecture Styles & Data-Sharing / Integration Patterns ~14% Specialty Ch 10
Specialty subtotal ~70% Specialty Ch 10
Data Governance of R&MD ~8% Supporting Ch 3
Data Quality (matching, profiling, dimensions) ~9% Supporting Ch 13
Data Integration & Interoperability (feeding the hub) ~7% Supporting Ch 8
Data Modeling / Architecture / Metadata of R&MD ~6% Supporting Ch 4, 5, 12
Supporting subtotal ~30% Supporting Ch 3, 8, 13, 4/5/12

Key insight: ~70% is Reference & Master Data (Ch 10) at application depth; ~30% tests how the supporting KAs feed, govern, and consume master and reference data. Matching/identity/survivorship is the single heaviest specialty cluster.

R&MD Core Definitions & Frameworks (Memorize Exactly)

These are the canonical, frequently-tested facts. Know them close to verbatim.

The 3 Goals of Reference & Master Data Management (DMBOK2)

  1. Ensure the organization has complete, consistent, current, and authoritative master and reference data across organizational processes.
  2. Enable master and reference data to be shared across enterprise functions and applications.
  3. Lower cost and reduce complexity of data usage and integration through standards, common data models, and integration patterns.

MDM — Gartner Definition (cited by DMBOK2)

"Master Data Management is a technology-enabled discipline in which business and IT work together to ensure the uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, semantic consistency, and accountability of the enterprise's official shared master data assets."

DMBOK2 stresses MDM is a discipline (people + process + technology), not simply a tool or a one-time project.

Guiding Principles (DMBOK2)

  • Shared Data — reference and master data must be managed so they are shareable across the organization.
  • Ownership — reference and master data belong to the organization, not to a particular application or department.
  • Quality — managed with ongoing data-quality measurement and stewardship.
  • Stewardship — business stewards are accountable for definitions, values, and quality.
  • Controlled Change — especially for reference data, value changes are governed, versioned, and effective-dated.
  • Authoritative Source — consumers use the designated system of record / system of reference, not ad-hoc copies.

The 6 MDM Activities — Detailed Reference

DMBOK2 frames master data management as a sequence of activities. Master the purpose of each — the exam asks "which activity does this scenario describe?" far more than "list all six."

# Activity Purpose
1 Define MDM Drivers & Requirements Establish why MDM is needed (single view, integration cost, compliance, analytics) and which entities are in scope. Prioritize subject areas by business value and pain.
2 Evaluate & Assess Data Sources Profile candidate source systems for each entity: coverage, quality, identifiers, overlap, authority. Decide which sources contribute and how trustworthy each is.
3 Define the Architectural Approach Choose the hub approach — DMBOK2's Registry / Transaction Hub / Consolidated (plus Coexistence as a common Gartner-style variant) — based on control needs, latency, intrusiveness, and how master data will be consumed.
4 Model Master Data Define the entities, identifiers, attributes, hierarchies/affiliations, and relationships. Establish the canonical/conceptual model and the cross-reference (xref) structure.
5 Define Stewardship & Maintenance Processes Establish how records are created, matched, merged/linked, corrected, and retired; who stewards them; how survivorship and exceptions are handled day-to-day.
6 Establish Governance Policies to Enforce Use Put policy and oversight in place so systems actually consume the master data (not bypass it); manage reference-data change; monitor quality and adoption.

Exam tip: Activities 2 (source assessment) and 3 (architecture choice) are heavily scenario-tested. "An organization has five customer systems of varying quality and wants minimal disruption to sources — what should it do FIRST / which style fits?" → assess sources, then often Registry for minimal intrusion.

MDM Key Processing Steps — Detailed Reference (DMBOK Figure 76)

Distinct from the program-level 6 MDM activities, DMBOK2 names the runtime data-pipeline steps that build and maintain master data. Know these five, in order:

# Step What happens
1 Data Model Management Resolve "system speak" — define enterprise-level terms/definitions and attribute granularity that make sense across the org, not per source system
2 Data Acquisition Receive/evaluate new sources; rapid match + DQ assessment; assess integration complexity; pilot impact on match rules; set DQ metrics and ownership
3 Data Validation, Standardization & Enrichment Validation (remove provably bad values), Standardization (conform to reference values/formats), Enrichment (add attributes, e.g., DUNS, to improve resolution)
4 Entity Resolution & Identifier Management Decide whether two references are the same entity; match → link or merge → assign a global identifier; manage IDs and affiliations
5 Data Sharing & Stewardship Publish/share master data to consumers and steward it over time

These steps culminate in the entity-resolution pipeline in the Matching section below. Don't confuse them with the 6 MDM activities (which set up the program) — these are the data-processing steps. Entity resolution itself = reference extraction → reference preparation → reference resolution → identity management → relationship analysis.

Reference Data Management — Deep Reference

Reference data is data used to characterize or classify other data, or to relate data to information beyond the organization's boundaries. It is the smaller, slower-changing, shared vocabulary that gives meaning to master and transactional data. (Example: a customer record's country_code = 'QA' only has meaning via the ISO 3166 reference set.)

Reference Data vs. Master Data (often confused)

Aspect Reference Data Master Data
What it is Codes, classifications, value sets that describe/categorize Business entities (customers, products) that participate in transactions
Examples Country codes, currency codes, status codes, gender codes, units of measure, industry classifications Customer, Product, Supplier, Employee, Account, Location
Change rate Slow, controlled, low volume Continuous, higher volume
Created by Often external standards bodies (ISO) or internal definition The organization's operational processes
Key risk Proliferation of local code sets; mapping drift Duplicates; conflicting versions of the truth

Reference Data Types — Chisholm's Six-Layer Taxonomy

DMBOK2 presents reference data using Malcolm Chisholm's six-layer taxonomy. Memorize the six layers — they are a frequent exam target:

Layer Description Examples
1. Internal Created and maintained within the enterprise Department codes, internal status / cost-center codes
2. Industry Standards set by industry groups SIC codes, SWIFT codes
3. National Standards set by national bodies State/province codes, ZIP/postal codes
4. International Standards set by international bodies ISO 3166 (country), ISO 4217 (currency), ISO 639 (language)
5. Third-Party Commercially supplied reference data D&B DUNS numbers
6. Derived Created by combining/transforming other reference data A region grouping derived from country + national codes

Two framings, both testable: Chisholm's six layers (above) classify reference data by source authority. DMBOK2 §1.3.2 separately lists its own reference-data categories (below) — so "geographic" and "computational" are DMBOK reference-data categories even though they are not Chisholm layers.

DMBOK2's Reference Data Categories (§1.3.2.2–1.3.2.6)

Category Description / example
Proprietary / Internal Created to support internal processes; grows organically; stewards balance common terms vs. local flexibility
Industry Created/maintained by industry associations or government bodies (e.g., ICD, NAICS) — a prerequisite for sharing & interoperability
Geographic / Geo-statistical Classification/analysis by geography (census demographics; weather mapped to geography) for planning & research
Computational Underpins common calculations (e.g., FX rates); changes frequently, so often purchased from third parties to avoid latency issues
Standard Reference Data Set Metadata Metadata about a reference set: Formal/Internal Name, Data Provider & source, provider version/date, internal version & reconciliation dates

Reference Data Structures (from simplest to richest)

Structure What it does Example
Simple code set / list Code + description (and maybe a definition) M = Male, F = Female
Cross-reference (xref) code set Maps one code set to another (proprietary ↔ standard, or system ↔ system) Legacy 1/2/3 status → standard ACTIVE/INACTIVE/PENDING
Hierarchy Parent–child roll-up relationships Region → Country → City
Taxonomy Classification tree with defined levels Product category taxonomy
Ontology Richest: concepts + relationships + rules (semantic) A knowledge model relating products, materials, and uses

Industry Standard Code Sets to Know (headline examples)

Standard Governs
ISO 3166 Country codes (e.g., QA, US, GB)
ISO 4217 Currency codes (e.g., QAR, USD, EUR)
ISO 639 Language codes
NAICS / SIC Industry / sector classification
ICD (medical) Diagnostic codes — ICD-9 ≈ 13,000 codes; ICD-10 ≈ 68,000 codes (expanded specificity)

Best practice: adopt recognized standards rather than inventing internal equivalents; this lowers integration cost and improves external interoperability — a direct expression of R&MD Goal 3. Memorize the ICD-9 (~13k) vs ICD-10 (~68k) contrast — it appears as a concrete exam fact.

Reference Data Change Management (a frequent exam theme)

Reference data is small but high-impact — a single code change can cascade across every system that uses it. Mature RDM requires:

  1. Clear ownership — a named steward owns each code set.
  2. Controlled change process — request → review → approve → version → publish → communicate.
  3. Effective dating / versioning — values have validity periods; never silently overwrite.
  4. Deprecation, not deletion — retire codes carefully; preserve history for old transactions.
  5. Mapping maintenance — keep cross-reference sets current as standards evolve.

Common RDM Challenges

  • Local code-set proliferation — every system invents its own status codes → mapping nightmare.
  • Mapping drift — cross-references go stale when a standard updates.
  • Ownership ambiguity — no one is accountable for a shared code set.
  • Uncontrolled change — a code added/changed without governance breaks downstream reports.

Reference Data Management Activities (DMBOK §2.2 — parallel the 6 MDM activities)

DMBOK2 covers MDM and Reference Data activities separately but with parallel structure. Reference data is smaller and less volatile and does not require matching / merging / linking, so its activities focus on sourcing, defining, and controlling change rather than entity resolution:

# RDM Activity Purpose
1 Define Drivers & Requirements Drivers are operational efficiency + higher data quality; the most important reference-data sets drive the RDM-system requirements
2 Assess Data Sources Decide buy (vendor, with guaranteed scheduled updates) vs. internal; identify, compare, assess internal sources; secure owner buy-in to central stewardship
3 Define Architectural Approach Account for volatility, update frequency, consumption models, history retention, a straightforward manual-update interface, and approval workflows
4 Model Reference Data Sets Model the sets (much reference data is more than code+description) to capture relationships, metadata, and data-quality rules
5 Define Stewardship & Maintenance Processes Stewards keep values complete/current and definitions clear; capture set-level metadata; run review/approval workflows
6 Establish Reference Data Governance Policies Mandate use of the central repository (directly, or via a system of reference populated from it) and govern quality

Exam contrast: if a stem involves matching, survivorship, or golden records, it's master data; if it involves code values, classifications, cross-references, or controlled value changes, it's reference data.

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "What distinguishes reference data from master data?" (Answer: reference data characterizes/classifies other data; master data are the business entities in transactions)
  • "An organization has 6 systems each with its own customer-status codes. What reference-data structure resolves this?" (Answer: a cross-reference (xref) code set mapping each to a standard set)
  • "Why adopt ISO 3166 instead of an internal country list?" (Answer: standardization lowers integration cost and improves interoperability — R&MD goal)
  • "A status code was changed in production and broke downstream reports. What RDM control was missing?" (Answer: reference-data change management — controlled change, versioning, communication)

Master Data Subject Areas — Detailed Reference

Master data clusters into recognizable subject areas. Know the taxonomy and the characteristic challenges of each.

Subject Area Examples Characteristic Challenge
Party (the biggest) Customer, Employee, Vendor/Supplier, Citizen, Patient One real-world person/org appears many times across systems → matching & identity resolution; party-role modeling (same party, multiple roles)
Product / Item Internal products, external/market products, SKUs Rich attributes, categories, variants; managed via PIM
Financial Accounts, cost centers, GL structures, budgets Roll-up hierarchies; regulatory accuracy
Location Addresses, sites, geographies Standardization, geocoding, address validation, hierarchies
Asset Equipment, property, IT assets Lifecycle, ownership, and location tracking
Contract / Policy Contracts, agreements, insurance policies Relationships to parties and products
Rule Business rules referenced across systems Consistency and version control
Concept Classifications (e.g., industry/market concepts) Overlaps with reference data; semantic consistency

Party Master Data & the Party-Role Model

The Party subject area is the heart of most MDM programs. Key concept: a Party (a person or organization) is modeled once, and roles (customer, employee, vendor, citizen) are relationships attached to that party. This avoids duplicating the same person as separate "customer" and "employee" records.

MDM Specializations

Specialization Focus Notes
Customer Data Integration (CDI) Party/customer master The classic "single view of customer"; matching-intensive
Product Information Management (PIM) Product master Attribute-rich; supports e-commerce, catalogs, syndication

Exam Relevance

  • "Same individual is both an employee and a customer. How should master data model this?" (Answer: one Party with two roles — not two separate master records)
  • "Which MDM specialization addresses 'single view of customer'?" (Answer: CDI)
  • "An e-commerce firm needs consistent, attribute-rich product data across channels. Which specialization?" (Answer: PIM)

Matching, Identity Resolution & Survivorship — Detailed Reference

Matching Approaches

Approach How it works When used Trade-off
Deterministic Exact / rule-based comparison (equal keys, exact field rules) Clean, reliable identifiers exist Fast, transparent; misses fuzzy duplicates (more false negatives)
Probabilistic Statistical scoring; weighted attribute agreement; thresholds Noisy data, no reliable key (typical for party) Catches fuzzy matches; needs tuning; risk of false positives

Match Rule Types (nail the merge-vs-link distinction)

Rule type What it does
Duplicate-identification match rules Identify records that are likely the same entity
Match-merge rules Combine matched records into a single consolidated record (survivorship applied; sources may be collapsed)
Match-link rules Link/cross-reference matched records without merging — records stay separate but are connected via an identifier/xref

Why it's tested: Merge is destructive/consolidating; link is non-destructive (keeps sources intact, connects them). Registry-style MDM relies on linking; consolidation-style relies on merging.

Match Errors

Error Meaning Plain language Business cost example (biometric identity)
False positive Two records matched that are not the same entity Over-matching Two different citizens merged into one identity → one person's records wrongly attached to another (severe)
False negative Two records that are the same entity not matched Under-matching One citizen appears as two identities → duplicate benefits/credentials

Tuning trades these off (loosening rules reduces false negatives but increases false positives). For high-stakes identity, false positives are usually the more dangerous error.

Survivorship / Consolidation

When records are merged, survivorship rules decide which attribute values "win" into the golden record:

  • Most recent (latest update wins)
  • Most trusted source (source-priority ranking)
  • Most complete (non-null / longest / richest value)
  • Highest confidence / trust score

The output is the golden record — though DMBOK cautions the term can be misleading because a single "truth" may not exist for every attribute; some implementations keep a "best version" assembled per-attribute.

End-to-End Identity Resolution Pipeline

Source records
   ↓  Standardize / cleanse (normalize names, addresses, formats)
   ↓  Match (deterministic and/or probabilistic)
   ↓  Link (xref, keep separate)  OR  Merge (consolidate)
   ↓  Apply survivorship → Golden record / best version
   ↓  Distribute / publish to consumers (per architecture style)

Exam Relevance

  • "Records are connected but kept separate in their source systems. Which rule type?" (Answer: match-link)
  • "Two distinct customers were combined into one record. What error is this?" (Answer: false positive / over-match)
  • "Which survivorship rule keeps the value from the highest-priority system?" (Answer: most-trusted-source)
  • "Probabilistic matching is chosen over deterministic when…?" (Answer: reliable unique identifiers are absent / data is noisy)

MDM Architecture / Data-Sharing Approaches — Detailed Reference

Exam framing matters here. DMBOK2 Ch 10 names three basic approaches to implementing a Master Data hub: Registry, Transaction Hub, and Consolidated. The broader industry (Gartner) often lists implementation styles that also include Coexistence and Centralized. For a DMBOK2-based exam, lead with the three DMBOK approaches and recognize the Gartner styles as variants. "Which approach fits this scenario?" is a signature question.

DMBOK2's Three Approaches (primary — memorize these)

Approach Where master data lives DMBOK2 description Pros Cons
Registry Stays in the systems of record; the hub is an index of identifiers / cross-references pointing to sources Access to master data comes from the master index; sources remain authoritative Easy to implement; few changes to sources; least invasive Complex queries to assemble a record from many systems; semantic-difference rules implemented in many places
Transaction Hub In the hub only; applications interface with the hub to access/update master data The hub is the system of record for master data Strongest governance; single consistent source; business rules in one place Costly to remove update capability from existing sources; most intrusive
Consolidated SORs keep local copies; master data is consolidated into a common repository / data-sharing hub (the system of reference) Hybrid of Registry + Transaction Hub; enterprise view served from the hub Enterprise view with limited impact on sources Data replication and latency between hub and sources

The Gartner Implementation Styles (recognize as variants)

Style Maps to / adds
Registry = DMBOK Registry
Consolidation = DMBOK Consolidated (often analytics/reporting-focused; pushed downstream to the DW)
Coexistence Mastered in a hub and synchronized bidirectionally with sources — not a separate DMBOK "approach," but commonly tested
Transaction / Centralized = DMBOK Transaction Hub; the hub is the single authoritative source apps use directly

How to Choose (decision drivers)

  • How much can you disrupt sources? Little → Registry; a lot → Transaction Hub.
  • Need an enterprise/analytics view with limited source impact, latency acceptable? → Consolidated.
  • Need to write mastered values back to sources? → Coexistence or Transaction Hub.
  • Latency tolerance? Batch is fine → Consolidated / Registry; near-real-time operational → Coexistence / Transaction Hub.

Data Sharing, Latency & Integration

  • The data-sharing hub is the MDM backbone; integration patterns (ETL/ELT, messaging/streaming, data services/APIs) feed and publish master data.
  • Latency matters: a Consolidated hub has inherent replication/latency vs. near-real-time Coexistence / Transaction Hub.
  • A canonical model (shared, neutral data model) reduces point-to-point mapping between systems.

Exam Relevance

  • "DMBOK names which three approaches to a Master Data hub?" (Answer: Registry, Transaction Hub, Consolidated)
  • "An index points to master data left in the systems of record — which approach?" (Answer: Registry)
  • "The hub is the system of record; apps update master data only in the hub — which approach?" (Answer: Transaction Hub)
  • "A common repository serves an enterprise view but sources keep local copies (with latency) — which approach?" (Answer: Consolidated)
  • "Master data is synced bidirectionally between a hub and the sources — which (Gartner) style?" (Answer: Coexistence)

Key Terms & Concepts — Quick Reference

Term DMBOK-aligned meaning
MDM (Gartner definition) A technology-enabled discipline in which business and IT ensure uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, semantic consistency, and accountability of shared master data
Master data Data about business entities that provide context for transactions (the "nouns")
Reference data Data used to characterize/classify other data or relate it to external information
Chisholm's 6 layers Reference-data taxonomy: Internal, Industry, National, International, Third-Party, Derived
Transactional data Data describing business events (the "verbs")
Golden record The single best/authoritative version of a master entity (DMBOK cautions the term)
System of Record (SOR) The authoritative source where data originates / is mastered
System of Reference A reliable, authoritative source that is not the original SOR but is trusted for use
Trusted source A recognized "best version of the truth"
Single view / single source of truth One consistent, reconciled view of an entity across the org
Canonical model A shared, neutral data model reducing point-to-point mappings
Data provenance / lineage Where data came from and how it was transformed
Reconciliation Resolving differences between sources to a consistent value
Survivorship Rules determining which values persist into the golden record

R&MD Drivers, Business Case & ROI

Why organizations invest in MDM/RDM:

Driver Business impact
Single view of entity (customer/product) Better service, cross-sell, accurate analytics
Reduced integration cost & complexity Canonical model + shared master cuts point-to-point mappings
Risk & compliance Accurate party/identity data for KYC, privacy, regulatory reporting
Operational efficiency Fewer duplicates → less rework, correct billing/shipping
M&A integration Reconcile duplicate customers/products across merged entities
Analytics / AI readiness Clean master data is the foundation for trustworthy analytics

ROI framing (same discipline as the DG plan): quantify duplicate-reduction savings, avoided rework, compliance-risk avoidance, and faster integration. Express benefits in cost-avoidance and efficiency terms; payback often comes from deduplication and integration savings.

Data Quality Integration with R&MD

Master data is the highest-priority data-quality domain — errors cascade across every process. DQ and R&MD are tightly coupled:

  • DQ dimensions for master data: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and especially uniqueness (no duplicates).
  • Profiling assesses source quality during Activity 2 (assess sources).
  • Matching/dedup is a DQ technique central to MDM.
  • Standards are stricter for master data (often 99%+; uniqueness target effectively 100%).
  • Who sets vs. executes: the Master Data Steward sets quality standards; DQ analysts implement rules/profiling and report metrics; issues escalate through governance.

Exam angle: "Why are master-data quality standards stricter than transactional?" (Answer: master data is shared context; errors propagate everywhere, with high business impact).

Data Governance of Reference & Master Data

R&MD without governance fails — systems bypass the hub and duplicates return. Governance provides:

  • Master Data Steward — cross-functional, often senior; accountable for an entity org-wide; resolves "what is the customer?" conflicts.
  • Ownership of reference data — each code set has a named owner and a change-control process.
  • Policy to enforce use — Activity 6: mandate that systems consume master data rather than re-create it.
  • Stewardship & escalation — operational stewards resolve most issues; cross-unit conflicts escalate to a council.

Exam angle: "Sales and Finance disagree on what counts as a 'customer.' Who resolves it?" (Answer: the Master Data Steward, via governance — not IT).

Data Integration & Interoperability with R&MD

MDM is fundamentally an integration discipline:

  • Sources feed the hub via ETL/ELT, messaging/streaming, or data services/APIs.
  • Latency choices (batch vs near-real-time) drive the architecture style and freshness of the golden record.
  • Canonical model reduces N×N point-to-point mappings to N mappings to a shared model.
  • Publishing/distribution pushes mastered data to consumers per the chosen style (Registry assembles on read; Consolidation/Transaction push out).

Exam angle: "How does integration latency affect MDM?" (Answer: it determines whether master data is near-real-time (coexistence/transaction) or batch-refreshed (consolidation/registry), affecting freshness and architecture).

Data Architecture, Modeling & Metadata of R&MD

  • Architecture: MDM is a core enterprise-architecture capability; it sits between operational sources and analytical/consumer systems.
  • Modeling: master data modeling defines entities, identifiers, attributes, hierarchies/affiliations, and relationships (e.g., party-role). A conceptual/canonical model anchors shared meaning.
  • Metadata: business definitions (glossary), lineage/provenance, and reference-set documentation make master/reference data understandable and auditable. Metadata links each master attribute to its definition, source, and steward.

Exam angle: "What modeling construct lets one person be both customer and employee without duplication?" (Answer: party-role model).

R&MD Maturity, Implementation & Organizational Change

  • Maturity progresses from ad-hoc/local code sets and rampant duplicates → defined stewardship, hub, and standards → measured quality/adoption → optimized, embedded master data as an enterprise asset.
  • Implementation typically starts with one high-value subject area (often Party/Customer), proves value, then expands — mirroring the "start narrow, expand broad" pattern from DG.
  • Organizational change: the hardest part is getting systems and people to use the master data (adoption), not building the hub. Governance + change management drive adoption.

R&MD Metrics — Detailed Reference

DMBOK2 (§6.1) ties specific metrics to Reference & Master Data and the processes that support them. Know these seven:

Metric What it measures
Data quality & compliance DQ-dashboard confidence (%) that a subject-area entity/attribute is fit-for-purpose across the org
Data change activity Rate of change of data values (auditing lineage of trusted data); used to tune MDM match algorithms
Data ingestion & consumption Which systems contribute data and which business areas subscribe from the sharing environment
Service Level Agreements (SLAs) Adherence to SLAs for contributors/subscribers — signals support, technical, and data problems
Data Steward coverage Who (name/group) is responsible for content, and how often coverage is evaluated (finds gaps)
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Infrastructure, licenses, support staff, consulting, training, etc., applied consistently
Data sharing volume & usage Volume/velocity of data defined, ingested, and subscribed to/from the data-sharing environment

Complementary quality view (from the repo chapter summary): R&MD quality is also often described along Completeness, Coverage, Quality, Matching (precision/recall), Timeliness, and Usage — a useful lens, but on a DMBOK2-grounded exam the seven §6.1 metrics above are the authoritative list.

Exam angle: "Which metric flags whether systems actually contribute/consume the master data?" (Answer: Data ingestion & consumption / Data-sharing volume & usage). "Which captures the rate of change of values and helps tune match algorithms?" (Answer: Data change activity).

Tools & Techniques — Quick Reference

Category Examples / Purpose
Entity-resolution / matching engines Deterministic + probabilistic matching, survivorship, golden-record creation
Data-quality tools Profiling, standardization/cleansing, validation, monitoring
Data-integration tools ETL/ELT, messaging/streaming, data services/APIs to load and publish master data
Reference-data management tools / repositories Manage code sets, cross-references, versioning, distribution
Workflow & stewardship tools Change requests, approvals, issue resolution
Metadata / business-glossary tools Definitions, lineage/provenance, ownership for master & reference data

Tool implementations (DMBOK §3): data integration tools, data remediation tools, operational data stores (ODS), data-sharing hubs (DSH), and specialized MDM applications (often packaged for party / product / account).

DMBOK Techniques (§4)

Technique Essence
Adhere to Master Data Architecture Follow a proper reference architecture; the integration approach accounts for org structure, # of systems of record, governance, access/latency needs, and # of consumers
Monitor Data Movement Track data flow to show sharing/usage, capture lineage, aid root-cause analysis, reveal latency from source → consumption, and validate business rules/transformations
Manage Reference Data Change A shared resource cannot change arbitrarily (DG Council governs). 5 change types: row-level external, structural external, row-level internal, structural internal, new sets. Planned (scheduled) changes need less governance than ad hoc; always assess impact and communicate to consumers
Data Sharing Agreements Stipulate what data can be shared and under what conditions; driven by DG; involves architects, providers, stewards, developers, analysts, and compliance/privacy/security officers

Flashcard Topics — Master These Cold

Group A is core DMBOK2 Ch 10 (highest exam weight). Group B covers expanded application/scenario depth.

Group A — Core Chapter 10 (Foundational, Memorize Exactly)

  2. Reference data — exact definition

  4. 3 Goals of Reference & Master Data

  13. CDI vs PIM

  15. SOR vs System of Reference vs Trusted Source

  18. False positive (over-match) vs false negative (under-match)

  20. MDM hub approaches — DMBOK's 3 (Registry, Transaction Hub, Consolidated) + Gartner variants (Coexistence, Centralized) + best-fit each

  21. MDM Gartner definition — technology-enabled discipline (business + IT) ensuring uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, semantic consistency, accountability of shared master data

  22. 3 Goals of R&MD — complete/consistent/current/authoritative; shared across the enterprise; lower cost/complexity via standards & common models

Exam-Day Strategy

  • 100 questions, 90 minutes ≈ 54 seconds per question. Don't overthink.
  • It's open book — but don't rely on lookups for definitions; reserve the book for tricky scenarios. Pre-tab Chapter 10 sections (Reference Data, Matching, Architecture Styles).
  • Flag-and-skip uncertain questions; return at the end.
  • Answer in DMBOK terms, not vendor terms. Your biggest personal risk: choosing an answer that's "industry-true" but not "DMBOK-true." When two answers seem right, pick the one matching DMBOK's exact framing.
  • Merge vs link, false-positive vs false-negative, and the 3 hub approaches are high-frequency discriminators — be precise.
  • For "which activity / which style fits?" scenarios, identify the decision driver (disruption tolerance, write-back need, latency, analytics vs operational) before answering.
  • Reference-data questions are where you're weakest — read them carefully and slowly.
